## Preface to the Reader.
### Honored Reader!

I hereby present these little treatises of an unnamed philosopher, <term>Philalethes<note>A pseudonym meaning "Lover of Truth," likely referring to Eirenaeus Philalethes, a famous 17th-century alchemist whose identity remains debated.</note></term>, in the German language, which I first allowed to go out into the world some time ago in Latin. Since it has been sufficiently reported back to me how these works were highly praised, well-received, and greatly esteemed by many—especially by scholars and those particularly devoted to the <term>Alchemical science<note>The historical practice combining philosophy, chemistry, and metallurgy, aimed at transmuting base metals and finding a universal medicine.</note></term>—I have found cause and deemed it good to translate them into our worthy mother-tongue for the benefit and use of our dear Germans. My hope is that perhaps some faithful hearts and diligent workers might be strengthened in their good intentions, while others—the wandering ones—might finally be converted from their imaginary, arrogant thoughts and their unfounded <term>slop-works<note>original: "Sudel Wercken"; a derogatory term for the messy, unscientific, and often fraudulent experiments of "puffers" or false alchemists.</note></term>. To be sure, a few people may have criticized and rejected it; yet they surely did so out of a twisted judgment, as those who—out of extreme blindness and falsely imagined <term>experience<note>original: "Experienz"</note></term>—use their ignorance to dismiss the very thing through which they could and should have corrected their own errors;

# Preface.

<meta>catchword: Straßburg</meta>

For it cannot be denied that our *Philalethes*, having completed his work and happily reaped the <term>treasure<note>original: "Kleinod"; in an alchemical context, this refers to the Philosopher’s Stone or the successful completion of the "Great Work."</note></term>, speaks from certain experience. Others, meanwhile, must see to it how they direct their course within their self-chosen boundaries, so that they do not perhaps stumble at the very goal itself and squander their courage, hope, and property. 

Furthermore—and so that no one might think that *Philalethes* is not to be relied upon simply because he occasionally uses certain sayings and turns of phrase not commonly found among most of the old <term>alchemists</term>—I have, in order to prove that he is in agreement with the ancients in all (or at least in every main point), appended another small treatise. This, too, I present for the first time in the German language: namely, that of the monk, *Brother Ferrarius* <note>likely referring to Efferarius Monachus, an influential 14th-century alchemist</note>. 

He is named thus not only by <term>Combachius<note>Johann Combach (1585–1651), a German physician and philosopher who published several alchemical works.</note></term>, who most recently brought him more perfectly to light from a manuscript copy belonging to *Nicolaus Maius* (formerly a counselor to Emperor *Rudolf II* <note>Emperor Rudolf II (1552–1612) was a famous patron of the occult sciences and alchemy in Prague.</note> of most glorious memory), but is also cited under this name in the *Figured Rosary* <note>original: "Rosario figurato"; likely the *Rosarium philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical series of illustrations.</note> and by *Giovanni Battista Nazari*, according to the opinion of *Pierre Borel* <note>A French physician and bibliographer of alchemy.</note>. ## to the King’s Locked Palace.
### Preface of the Author.

As I, an unnamed lover of truth and a <term>philosopher<note>original: "Philosophus"; in the 17th century, this specifically referred to a "natural philosopher" or alchemist—one who studies the hidden laws of nature through experiment.</note></term>, obtained the secrets of medicine, chemistry, and nature in the year sixteen hundred and forty-five after the redemption of the world <note>A common way of saying 1645 A.D.</note>, being in the twenty-third year of my age: I decided to write this little treatise so that I might fulfill my duty toward the <term>Sons of Art<note>original: "Söhne der Kunst"; a traditional term for the community of sincere alchemical practitioners who seek the "Great Work."</note></term>, and extend a hand to those who are entangled in the labyrinth of error. I did this so that the possessors (<term>Adepts<note>original: "Adepti"; those who have successfully achieved the goal of alchemy, the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note></term>) might see that I am their equal and their brother; and that those, however, who have been led astray by the chatter of imposters, might see and seize the light by which they can surely return. I further surmise that not a few will be enlightened through this work of mine. These are no mere fables, but actual proofs which I have seen and performed, and of which I know; this an Adept will easily conclude and discern from these lines. Therefore, as I [have written] this for the [benefit]<note>The German text breaks here mid-word "Be-" and continues on the next page with the catchword "sten," forming "Besten" (benefit/best).</note> of my neighbor—

write most <note>The text begins mid-sentence from the previous page: "write most [clearly/honestly]."</note>: so let it be enough that I say publicly that no one who has written of this Art has ever written so clearly; and that I have several times laid aside my pen while writing, because I would have preferred to hide the truth under the mask of <term>envy<note>original: "Mißgunst"; in alchemical literature, the "Envy of the Sages" refers to the tradition of intentionally obscuring secrets to prevent them from falling into the hands of the unworthy or the wicked.</note></term>. ## Chapter VI.

### Concerning the Air of the Sages.

The expansion or the firmament of heaven is called the Air in Holy Scripture. Thus our <term>Chaos<note>In alchemy, "Chaos" refers to the raw, undifferentiated prime matter (materia prima) used at the beginning of the Great Work.</note></term> is also called Air, and this is not without a special mystery. For just as the firmamental Air is the separator of the waters; so likewise is our Air. Therefore, our work is in truth a <term>Microcosm<note>original: "Begriff der grossen Welt" (a concept or summary of the great world). The "Little World" that mirrors the "Macrocosm" of the universe.</note></term>. For as the waters under the firmament are to be seen, appearing to us who are upon the earth, yet the upper waters are hidden from our eyes because they are so far from us: so also in our Little World, the mineral waters which are outside the center are to be seen, but those which are locked within cannot indeed be seen with our eyes, yet they are nonetheless truly present. These are the ones of which the author of the *New Light* <note>original: *Novi Luminis*. This refers to Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), a famous alchemist who wrote *Novum Lumen Chymicum* (The New Chemical Light).</note> speaks, which indeed exist, but are not to be seen until it pleases the artist. Just as the air creates a distinction between the waters, so also our Air prevents all entry of the waters that are outside the center. For if they were to go inside and be mixed together, they would immediately combine through an inseparable union.

# The Closed Palace. Chapter XIII.
### C 4

Thus, no man is able to achieve anything alone, especially in works of **mercy**, unless he wishes to put his life in danger. I recently experienced this myself in several foreign places, where I gave **medicine** to some very sick, abandoned people burdened with miserable physical ailments, whereupon they immediately regained their health to great astonishment. 

Thereupon, a rumor immediately arose concerning the <term>Elixir of the Wise</term> <note>The "Elixir of the Wise" is the Philosopher's Stone in liquid form, said to be a universal panacea capable of curing any illness.</note>, so that more than once, with the greatest difficulty, I had to take flight by night in disguise—with a shorn head and false hair, as well as under different names. Otherwise, I would have fallen into the hands of wicked people who pursued me solely out of suspicion and a shameful **hunger for money**. I could relate many such stories, which would seem ridiculous to some. For they will say: "If I had this or that..."

## Chapter XV.
### Concerning the Incidental Purification of Mercury and Gold.

**Gold** is found perfect within the earth, and for this reason, it is sometimes found in small pieces and sand; if you can obtain it in this pure state, it is clean enough. If not, then purify it by means of **Antimony** <term>Antimony: A metallic element used in alchemy to "devour" impurities in gold, leaving the gold refined.</term>, or upon the test <term>Test: A cupel, or shallow porous bowl, used in cupellation to separate precious metals from base metals like lead.</term>, or boil it with **aqua fortis** <note>original: "aqua fort"; nitric acid.</note>, though you must first granulate the gold <term>Granulate: The process of pouring molten metal into water to create small, high-surface-area grains.</term>. Beyond this, however, it also requires an incidental purification to wipe away the external filth <note>original: "Unflat"; dross or surface impurities.</note> that it casts out from its center. This work is not strictly necessary, yet it accelerates the Work, and therefore it is not unserviceable. Take, therefore, your Mercury—which you have prepared through the appropriate number of Eagles—and sublimate it three times from common salt and iron scoria <note>original: "Eisenschlacken"; the slag or waste matter from smelting iron.</note>, rubbing it...

## Chapter XXV.
### Of the second Regime of the Work, which belongs to Saturn.

When the Regime of Mercury has been brought to an end—whose work it is to strip the King <note>The "King" is a common alchemical symbol for Gold or the perfected metal.</note> of his golden garments, and to occupy the Lion <note>The "Lion" represents the fixed, solid matter that must be dissolved.</note> with various struggles and to provoke him until he is entirely exhausted—then the Regime of Saturn begins. For God wills that the work once begun should come to its proper end; and it is to be noted in this operation that the exit of one is the entrance of the other, the end of one is the origin of the other. The Regime of Mercury does not end so soon that its successor, Saturn, does not immediately appear, who attains the regime by right of succession. When the Lion dies, the Crow <note>The "Crow" or Raven is the classic symbol for *Nigredo*, the stage of blackness and decay that must precede rebirth.</note> is born.

And this is a very uniform regime with regard to the heat. For here there is only one color, and indeed the very blackest; but there is no smoke, nor winds, nor any sign of life. ## Chapter XXVIII.

### Of the Regime of Venus.

## Chapter XXXIII.

### Brother Ferrarius

**Imagination**, by which they persuade themselves that they have found the truth, is for them sufficient; and yet it is all fantastical and not at all in accordance with reason—indeed, it is full of error and does not agree at all with the natural beginnings. For their head, which is full of **vapors** <note>original: "Dünste". In medieval physiology, "vapors" rising from the stomach or humors were believed to cloud the brain, leading to "fantasies" or irrational thoughts that prevent clear perception of reality.</note>, can neither understand nor grasp the true intention of natural things. 

We also find many of those who possess an unstable mind; they fall from one opinion to another, wanting now this, now that, just like those who believe one thing one moment and desire another the next, without the basis of any rational cause. Soon after, they believe something else and likewise desire something else again; these people are so inconsistent that they cannot or will not complete even the smallest thing they aim for, but rather leave it lying unfinished. 

There are also others who despise this **science** <term>science|From the German "Wissenschaft." In this period, it refers to a systematic body of knowledge or a "sacred art," specifically the study of nature's transformations (alchemy).</term> and do not believe at all that it exists. They cite the arguments of **Geber** <note>original: "Geber". The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a legendary polymath. His works were the foundation of medieval alchemy; here, Ferrarius notes that critics ironically use Geber's own rigorous standards to claim alchemy is impossible.</note> and others, according to which this science cannot exist, nor have any truth within it. Therefore, it remains for me to fulfill my promise to thwart the aforementioned arguments and to prove openly that they are false.

And first, I wish to show what qualities an **artist** <note>original: "Künstler". The alchemist was called an "artist" because they practiced the "Art" (Ars), working to perfect or complete the processes that nature began.</note> of this art must possess. For this purpose, I take the chapter from Geber as an example, as it were, which teaches all people a certain caution and

# Brother Ferrarius #

...mixture is dissolved, through a gradual and long-lasting **thickening** <term>thickening|original: "Eindickung." In alchemy, this is the process of inspissation, where a liquid substance is thickened into a solid through heat or evaporation.</term>, and a very well-tempered **cooking** <note>original: "Kochung." This refers to "decoction," the natural heat of the earth that matures or "ripens" minerals over long periods.</note> within their **mountain-fissures**; for which reason a **Philosopher** <note>Alchemical texts often cite "The Philosopher" (usually Aristotle, Hermes Trismegistus, or Geber) as an ultimate authority. The "dearest son" address is a hallmark of the Hermetic tradition.</note> says: "We give to you, dearest son, a general rule: that no thickening of any moist thing occurs unless the most subtle parts first smoke out from the moisture, and the coarse parts are retained from that moisture."

Thus, in this mixing, the dry surpasses the moist; and the true mixing of the dry and the moist is when the moist is tempered by the dry, and the dry by the moist, so that from them a single substance emerges that is uniform in its nature, and tempered between hard and soft. ### On the Effects of the Beginnings.

Now follows the explanation of the effects of the aforementioned beginnings, namely <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "Quecksilbers"; in alchemy, mercury is the "feminine" principle of liquidity and metallic luster.</note> and <term>sulfur</term> <note>original: "Schwefels"; the "masculine" principle of combustion and structure.</note>. For Lucas <note>A character in the *Turba Philosophorum* representing a philosopher (possibly a corruption of Leucippus or Chrysippus).</note> says in the *Turba Philosophorum* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum"; "The Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a record of a debate among ancient philosophers.</note>: You need nothing more than a single thing, and that same single thing is changed into a different nature in every degree of our work. Such degrees, however, follow the various divisions of the mixable elements that occur during its *operation*.

And they have called every division (or *proportion*) in its degree—according to the order that Nature maintains in the manner and progression of her birthing—by the name of a metal. In this regard, it is distinguished from common raw mercury, because its most subtle moisture or its superfluous **vaporous** <note>original: *vaporosisches*</note> essence has been evaporated out of this matter, and its nearby coarse parts are gathered together and thickened into a metallic hard **mass** <note>original: *Massa*</note> and perfectly mixed with a strong union with the dry. Mercury, however, lacks all of this, and therefore it cannot cling to the bodies in the ground of nature. 

The composition of this Stone comprises two pieces within itself: one **volatile** <term>volatile: *flüchtig*, a substance that easily evaporates or turns into gas when heated</term>, and the other **fixed** <term>fixed: *fix*, a substance that remains solid and stable even under extreme heat</term>. On account of the volatile part, it can be compared with mercury, but on account of the fixed part, it can be compared with the metals.

## The Treatise of the Whole Work.

The first work of this process is the **sublimation** <term>sublimation: *Sublimirung*, a process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then collected again as a solid, used here to "spiritualize" or purify the substance</term> of the work, namely the extraction of the spiritual part from the bodily, and the separation from the same, and the preservation of that purified spirit, or rather a cleansing and scouring of that which has been raised up through repeated sublimation, until it becomes entirely pure; for if the matter were not purified through sublimation, its density would prevent it from becoming a **medicine** <term>medicine: *Medicin*, a common alchemical term for the Philosopher's Stone or the elixir used to transform base metals</term>, as **Menaldus** <note>a speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous early alchemical text</note> says in the *Turba*: the thick earthly part does not **tincture** <term>tincture: *tingiret*, to chemically transform or "color" a metal into gold or silver</term>, but rather the subtle part of nature which is in the body, where it is transfigured and colored: therefore the ore does not color unless it is first colored itself.

**Alphidius** <note>an Arab alchemist often cited in medieval European texts</note> says: the fire should be between strong and mild, until the spirit departs from the body and thus rises on high, just as the clouds rise above the earth; thus the body will remain at the bottom of the vessel without spirit in it. And **Belus** <note>another figure from the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> in the *Turba*: The science of this art is nothing other than a vapor and a sublimation of water.

Thus the first work is the sublimation of this thing, or of the **soul** <note>original: *Seele*</note>, for it is called the soul by some **philosophers** <note>alchemical authors often referred to themselves collectively as "the Philosophers"</note>, as **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says, stating: Take the egg, and strike it with the fiery sword,

### Concerning the Fixation of the Matter through the Boiling of the Fire.

After the whole matter has become spiritual <note>referring to the substance being reduced to a vaporous or volatile state</note>, one must continue the boiling within it until it is fixed <term>figiret|From 'fixation'; the alchemical process of making a volatile, vaporous substance solid and resistant to heat</term> with the most perfect fixation, which withstands all trials of the fire. Among all the labors of the Stone, however, fixation is very common and well-known. For everyone knows that any medicine <note>In alchemy, the 'Medicine' refers to the Philosopher's Stone or the elixir at various stages of its development</note> that is not fixed cannot effect a complete transformation when it is cast upon a body <note>original: "Corpus"; referring to a base metal to be transmuted</note>. For because it is volatile <note>original: "flüchtig"</note> and cannot endure the trial of the fire during melting and glowing, it withdraws again from the body upon which it was cast, leaving the body in its former, or even a worse, state. And because the volatile medicine, when cast upon the bodies, also causes brittleness in them—as we see in common medicines with which our tinctures are made in a short time. That one must give this matter a fixity is also shown by **Parmenides** in the *Turba* <note>The 'Turba Philosophorum' (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting of pre-Socratic philosophers</note>, when he says:

## Concerning the first color, which is black, and concerning the governance of the fire therein.

Let no one be deceived by this chapter, for although it speaks of the beginning of the work and the first color, it is not to be understood as the first beginning of the entire work <note>The initial preparation of the raw materials</note>, but rather the second, when the *elixir* <term>elixir|The "Philosopher's Stone" in its developmental stage, intended to transform metals or heal the body</term> is composed from the fixed and the volatile <note>The "fixed" refers to substances that resist the heat of fire, while the "volatile" refers to those that easily evaporate or sublimate</note>. Thus the first color that appears in the *matter* <note>original: "Materie"</note> is black, since it appears at the beginning of the cooking; in this cooking, a gentle fire must indeed be used, so that the spiritual *matter* <note>The volatile, "spirit-like" components of the mixture</note> does not flee from it. 

Through gentle cooking, the unions and natures of the male and female <note>Alchemical metaphors for the active (Sulfur) and passive (Mercury) principles</note> are brought together and become one thing through constant boiling. The sign of this cooking is this first color which appears from both, as **Florus** says in the *Turba* <note>Referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note>: "The blackness has improved it, because it has made peace between the volatile and the non-volatile, and brought them into one." **Lilium** <note>Likely referring to the *Lilium Intelligentiae*, a common title for alchemical manuscripts</note> also speaks of this gentle cooking, saying: "The melting is to be repeated in the gentle fire so often, until..."

The author argues that glass is non-porous, preventing the escape of precious vapors.</note>, while other materials are not, because through their pores the substances are gradually diminished and disappear. Metals also do not serve for this purpose, because the spirits <term>Spiritus|In alchemy, "spirits" are volatile substances—such as mercury or sulfur—that easily vaporize and are prone to escaping the vessel if it is not perfectly sealed.</term>, due to their similarity [to the metal], penetrate into them and unite with them, and therefore they pass through and vanish. For this reason, the philosophers have wanted to use no other thing than glass. That is the entire description of the vessel, which I intend to present to Your Holiness in a drawing, because it would be difficult to understand from the words of the philosophers alone. For the philosophers have described the vessel in question after the manner of the natural vessel <note>A common alchemical metaphor for the womb, signifying that the chemical process within the glass mimics natural gestation and birth.</note>, and in this is accomplished the most precious secret, which is above all secrets of this world, and is an incomparable treasure. If you understand well everything that has been reported before, then that which Socrates <note>Medieval alchemical texts frequently attributed sayings to ancient Greek philosophers to provide a lineage of authority, though these quotes are usually apocryphal.</note> says will follow: "I have now shown you the governance of the White Stone <term>White Stone|The *albedo* or "whiteness" is the penultimate stage of the Great Work, representing a state of high purity and fixed stability.</term>, which is nothing other than 'women's work' and 'child's play' <note>original: "Werck der Weiber, und ein Kinder-Spiel" | A famous alchemical maxim (*opus mulierum et ludus puerorum*) implying that once the difficult initial stages are completed, the final cooking requires only patience and gentle, steady heat.</note>."

He must carefully observe the **experiments** <note>original: *experimente*; here meaning the practical laboratory operations</note> and their progress, changing and renewing them as reason advises him, until he sees the **signs** <note>the specific color changes, like the Black Sun or the White Swan, that indicate progress in the Great Work</note> described by the **Philosophers** <term>original: *Philosophis*; in this context, it specifically refers to historical alchemists</term>. Subsequently, he should set aside any erroneous works and apply himself solely to reaching completion. However, he must not let his courage fail even if he should err several times; yet he must guard himself against excessive expenses. Thus, through God’s blessing, he will finally be granted his wish. So that I may now instruct such a person, I have written the following true, clear, and perfect treatise without deception. I wish, however, to remind all greedy, deceitful, and other such rabble that they should leave both the **Art** and this treatise in peace,

# Concerning the Philosopher's Stone.

...is enclosed, which awakens the warmth in the body and cooks the moisture into a viscous or fatty powder <note>This "fatty powder" refers to the unctuous or oily state of the matter as it begins to thicken—a sign that the moisture is being "fixed" by the heat.</note>.

The reason this work precedes dissolution is as follows: Firstly, because a dissolution has already occurred through our divine water <note>original: "göttliches Wasser". This refers to the Philosophic Mercury, the primary solvent used to break down the raw materials at the very start of the process.</note>, so to speak. Therefore, the <term>coagulation</term> <note>The process where a liquid or volatile substance becomes solid or "fixed."</note> of the spirits must be expected immediately thereafter, because spirits are always coagulated after the body's dissolution. For they share the same operation; whatever the nature of the dissolution, a similar nature of coagulation is to be expected following it.

Secondly, the order of nature requires it. For first the Woman exercises her dominion, which must necessarily be overcome by her Husband; the Woman, however, retains her full dominion within the water. This, then, will be the first task of the Husband as he demonstrates his powers: that he must first overcome that in which the Woman possesses both of her qualities <note>The "Woman" (Mercury) is characterized by the qualities of Cold and Moisture. The "Husband" (Sulfur) must overcome these to bring stability to the matter.</note>. Once that is accomplished, he will easily make her submissive to him in that state where she possesses only one quality.

Finally, warmth is not necessarily established as a secondary property; rather, the dryness of the warmth will always be the ultimate goal. Therefore, the Husband must first demonstrate his powers, and for this reason, <term>Calcination</term> <note>original: "Calcinatio". The process of reducing a substance to a dry powder through heat; in alchemy, this represents the purification and "fixing" of the substance so it can no longer evaporate.</note> is rightly considered the beginning of the Work.

# OF THE PHILOSOPHER’S STONE.

...for they are one and the same: <term>Sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, Sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle of matter.</note> is <term>Mercury</term> <note>Mercury represents the passive, feminine, and fluid principle.</note> matured and cooked; Mercury is raw and immature Sulfur.

Therefore, this divine work of <term>Creation</term> <note>The alchemist views their work in the laboratory as a microcosm of God's creation of the universe.</note> must be observed: namely, how Nature has worked in the birthing of metallic bodies beneath the earth in the ore veins. Because in our work we follow her as closely as is ever possible, we also choose the same matter that she has used—although, to shorten the work and to achieve a more-than-perfect <term>exaltation</term> <note>original: "Erhöhung". This refers to the process of raising a substance to a higher state of purity or power.</note> of the Stone, <term>the Art</term> <note>original: "die Kunst". This almost always refers to Alchemy itself, the "Sacred Art."</note> has invented a far more subtle way of arrangement for her. For in the metallic veins, only one thing is found, namely Mercury, which is entirely raw and cold, and in which the sulfurous property is completely suppressed. There, almost no boiling heat is found; but through an imperceptible movement, over a long time, this metallic <term>principle</term> <note>original: "Principium".</note> is gradually changed until it is finally transformed into a fixed Sulfur. Thus, that which was called Mercury as long as it remained cold and moist is, in this its exaltation or awakening, called Sulfur.

In this work of ours, however, the matter behaves differently; for in addition to the raw and cold Mercury, we have something else: namely, matured <term>Gold</term>, in which the more active properties are actually present.

The signs of this, our <term>calcination: the process of reducing a substance to a fine powder, here referring to a spiritualized chemical change rather than simple burning</term>, are these: First, after the body has been saturated by the water, shortly after the <term>doorkeeper: <note>original: "Thorhüter" — in alchemy, this often symbolizes the first degree of heat or the specific substance that allows entry into the Work.</note></term> awakens the heat of the bath, the water—or the compound which was previously shining—begins to grow dark. ->### On the Philosopher’s Stone<-
<note>original: "von dem Stein der Weisen."</note>

...[could] lead to despair. Now, when we speak of our works, do not believe that we accomplish them in one or two days, or that we get to see colors or signs immediately in the first hour: truly not so; rather, we have toiled for a very great and long time until a compatibility appeared between the conflicting properties. For this reason, **Trevisanus** <note>Bernard of Treviso, a famous 15th-century Italian alchemist known for his long search for the Stone</note>, a man learned and pious in this art, teaches in his *Practice* <note>original: "Praxi"</note> that he remained in the **prison**—that is, in the doubt and uncertainty of his mind—for forty days, but afterwards came to himself again and saw clouds and fog. Indeed, if you throw a little grain into good soil for me, you do not clear away the earth every day to look and see if and how much it has grown; for if you did that, you could not expect even a decent sprouting or greening, let alone any fruit from it.

Some are so foolish and senseless that, as soon as they have joined the **substance to be dissolved** <note>original: "Aufzulösende"</note> with the solvent, they immediately look for signs of the effects, and cannot be content unless they either move the **Work** <term>the Work: the "Magnum Opus" or the specific chemical process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term>, or open it, or add something to it, or take something away, or at the very least increase the fire so that they might accelerate the Work, and in this way [hinder]...

Regarding this, hear what **Flamel** <note>original: "Flamellus"; refers to Nicolas Flamel, a legendary 14th-century figure associated with the discovery of the Philosopher's Stone</note> says: "The color that you shall first see is the blackness—and not just any blackness, but the very blackest of coal—and this within forty days." **Ripley** <note>original: "Riplæus"; refers to George Ripley, an influential 15th-century English alchemist and author of *The Compound of Alchymy*</note> says the very same: "Let the mixed and united natures lie together for six weeks to conceive, a time which you should wait out with a gentle fire." However, understand all of this to mean the blackness in its highest degree, which can also be seen from the words of **Flamel** repeated above; but the lesser blackness will appear sooner. Thus says the *Ladder of the Sages* <note>original: "Leiter der Weisen," referring to the *Scala Philosophorum*, an alchemical treatise detailing the steps of the Great Work</note> concerning the degree of **Putrefaction** <term>Putrefaction: *Putrefactio*, a vital stage where the substance "dies" and decomposes, turning black before it can be purified and reborn</term>: "Within sixteen days, while maintaining a gentle fire, the **Matter** <term>Matter: *Materia*, the physical substance undergoing transformation within the alchemical vessel</term> will be constantly covered with a blackness; and this occurs sooner or later, according to the worker’s skill in the joining together of the materials."

# Concerning the Philosopher's Stone

But do intermediate colors also appear in the progression from whiteness to blackness, just as they do in the progression from blackness to whiteness? It appears so, because one cannot move from one extreme to another without passing through the middle. And we answer that they do appear thus, although in an irregular manner; and some will appear in one work during the progression to the highest degree of blackness, which perhaps will not appear in another, namely because they are merely accidental colors <note>In alchemy, "accidental colors" are transient hues, like those on a peacock's tail, that appear as the material changes but are not the primary goal of the stage.</note>: but they are not quite the same between the first whiteness and blackness as those found between this and the final whiteness, for the condition of the matter is not the same there. In the first, it was thick and more earthly, requiring burning and purification; but in this work, the matter <note>original: "Materia"</note> is more spiritual and pure. Therefore, in the pure or purified subject <term>subject: the underlying base material or "prime matter" undergoing the transformation</term>, in the progression from the furthest blackness to the furthest whiteness, the intermediate colors will be much lighter and more wonderful than those which appear in the earthly subject. They will appear in both progressions; in the first passage between the extremes, they will be darker, fewer, and uglier; in the latter, however, they will be more bright and shining, according to the philosopher’s testimony <note>original: "Philosophi Zeugnuß"</note>. After the highest blackness and before the whiteness, in the hour of union, the greatest wonders shall appear. For as many colors as can be [imagined] in the whole world...

**Cohobation** <note>original: "Cohobirung"; the process of repeatedly distilling a liquid and pouring it back onto the solid residue to extract more "virtue" or essence.</note>, or repeated infusion, is a soaking, a feeding, and a moistening of the earth; this occurs through heat until the dry matter finally begins to **coagulate**, which is called the thickening. Through prolonged cooking or **sublimation**, this process introduces **fixity** <note>The state where a substance becomes stable under heat and no longer evaporates.</note>, the end of which is **exaltation** <note>The refinement of a substance to increase its potency or "noble" qualities.</note>. This is not a spatial change from a lower place to a higher one, but rather the act of making the most noble thing out of something lowly.

These are all our labors and the successive *dispositions* <note>original: "Dispositiones"; the specific arrangements or chemical states of the matter.</note>, which some call "governments." Whoever wishes to give them such a name is free to do so; nevertheless, he should know that there is only a twofold fire, namely a natural and a fire against nature. The latter works first, for the former is brought to light only through the latter. **Putrefaction** <note>The breakdown of the substance, usually indicated by it turning black; considered a necessary "death" before a chemical "rebirth."</note> must precede **rebirth**. Because these two fires contend with one another, they create the **unnatural fire**, and from this strife arises putrefaction. Afterward, however, the rebirth becomes glorious, wherein the sulfur and the water become one, and they receive their **coagulation** from none other than the natural fire.

Thus our body, which is commonly called the **Lemnian Earth** <note>A famous medicinal red clay from the island of Lemnos, used here as an alchemical metaphor for the "fixed" or solid part of the matter.</note>, accomplishes everything—but by no means if it is not with

It explains the transition from the "death" of putrefaction to a glorious rebirth where sulfur and water are permanently united.</summary>

## Philaletha’s Third Part

...the government; the weight is twofold, and the government is also twofold: those which perform these works, such as <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or ash.</note>, <term>dissolution</term> <note>The melting or liquefying of a solid substance.</note>, <term>separation</term> <note>Isolating the pure essence of a substance from its "dross" or impurities.</note>, <term>conjunction</term> <note>The union of the separated elements.</note>, <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The breakdown of the matter, often called the "death" of the substance, marked by a black color.</note>, <term>distillation</term> <note>A process of purification where liquid is evaporated and then condensed.</note>, <term>coagulation</term> <note>The process of a liquid thickening or becoming solid.</note>, <term>sublimation</term> <note>The transition of a substance directly from a solid to a vapor, used here to elevate the "spirit" of the matter.</note>, <term>fixation</term> <note>Rendering a substance stable so that it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to heat.</note>, and <term>exaltation</term> <note>The final refinement that increases the potency and "nobility" of the chemical stone.</note>: 

Among these, the first two works occur primarily by means of the first fire’s moderate, non-burning, and altering or changing heat, which warms the "Bath of the King" <note>A metaphor for the solvent or environment where the primary material—the King—undergoes its first transformation.</note> and transforms him—initially into a subtle, viscous, divided, black, and stinking earth, and thereafter into a variegated mineral water. This fire is called a "fire against nature" <note>original: "Feuer wider die Natur"; a technical term for the external, artificial heat provided by the alchemist's furnace.</note>. 

The three following works occur through the joining together of the first and third fires, namely the natural fire and the fire against nature: which, when thus combined, create an "unnatural fire." In this state, the matter daily circulates, and the more subtle part is separated from the thick, until everything attains the same temperament; at that point, it reunites what was separated, impregnates it, and thus brings it into <term>putrefaction</term>. 

The final five works are performed by the "fire of nature," which grows daily and gains the upper hand. It initially drives the putrefied matter around each day and cleanses it of the dregs or impurities through frequent ascending and descending <note>Refers to the movement of vapors rising and falling within the sealed glass vessel.</note>; for this reason, it is called a <term>distillation</term>, <term>volatilization</term>, <term>washing</term>, and <term>purification</term>.

<term>Cohobation</term> <note>original: "Cohobirung"; the process of repeatedly redistilling a liquid by pouring it back onto the solid matter remaining in the flask.</note>, or repeated infusion, is a saturating, a feeding, and a moistening of the Earth; and this is performed by the heat until finally the dry matter begins to <term>coagulate</term> <note>original: "coaguliren"; the process of a liquid thickening or becoming solid.</note>, which is called the thickening. Through prolonged boiling or <term>sublimation</term> <note>original: "Sublimirung"; the process where a substance is heated until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify the "spirit" of the matter.</note>, this introduces <term>fixity</term> <note>original: "Fixität"; the state where a substance is stable and no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to fire.</note>, the end of which is <term>exaltation</term> <note>original: "Erhöhung"; the final refinement that increases the potency and "nobility" of the alchemical stone.</note>. This is not a spatial change from a lower place to a higher one, but rather the making of the most noble thing out of a lowly thing.

These are all our works and sequential <term>dispositions</term> <note>original: "Dispositiones"; the specific arrangements or stages of the chemical process.</note>, which are called by some the "governments" <note>Also known as "regimens," these are stages of the alchemical process governed by different planetary or elemental forces.</note>: whoever wishes to give them such a name is free to do so; nevertheless, he should know that there is only a twofold fire, namely a natural and an unnatural one. The latter works first, for the former is brought to light only through the latter; and <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "Fäulung"; the chemical breakdown or "death" of the matter, necessary before a new form can arise.</note> must precede the rebirth. Because these two struggle with one another, they create the "unnatural fire," and from this strife arises the putrefaction. Afterward, however, the rebirth becomes glorious, wherein the <term>sulfur</term> <note>original: "Schwefel"; in alchemy, sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle of a substance.</note> and the water become one, and they receive their coagulation from none other than the natural fire.

Thus our Body—which is commonly called <term>Lemnian Earth</term> <note>original: "Lemnische Erde"; historically a medicinal clay from the island of Lemnos, used here as a metaphor for the purified, fertile "earth" or base of the alchemical work.</note>—accomplishes everything, but by no means if it is not with [our...] <meta>catchword: our (unserm)</meta>

### Third Part of Philaletha

This mountain, of which we are now speaking, is of a very warm temperature because it lies not far from the sun, and within this mountain is enclosed the vapor or spirit which is very necessary for our work. However, it does not rise up unless it is made alive, and it is not made alive unless one digs knee-deep into the earth at the summit of the mountain. But when that happens, the spirit or a very thin steam rises up, which is coagulated by the air and runs down drop by drop into a clear, pure water that is made warm like a bath, which is then immediately collected. For it is the true <term>Herald’s Staff of Mercury</term> <note>original: "Herolds-Stab des Mercurii." Also known as the caduceus, this symbol represents the power to mediate between opposing forces and is a tool for transformation in alchemical practice.</note> with which he works wonders. 

This is our water, our vessel, our fire, and our furnace; and it is our <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurius." Not the common liquid metal, but the "Philosophical Mercury," a refined substance believed to be the life-force of all matter.</note>—not the common kind, but rather a moisture of the purest salt, warm and damp, which we call Mercury. Because when compared with gold it is immature and cold, I tell you truly: had the Almighty not created this Mercury, the transformation of metals would be impossible. Thus is now our **Stone**, which all **Philosophers** seek, and in which are the first elements of the **minerals**, and the **Tincture**, the **Lime** <note>original: "Kalck" (calx); the crumbly substance produced when a metal or mineral is reduced by fire.</note>, the **Spirit**, the **Body**, and the **Soul**, the fixed and the volatile, the **Mercury**: not just any mercury, but that one with which **Nature** first begins her working, and has determined or ordered it through the first workings toward a **metallic nature**, but has left it imperfect.

So, if you will extract this **Stone** from the thing in which it is found, and if the **Art** <note>In this context, "Art" refers to Alchemy—the human intervention that completes what nature began.</note> begins there where **Nature** has left it <note>The original German says "vollkommen gelassen," which literally means "left perfect," but in this context implies nature has finished its specific stage of development, leaving the rest to the alchemist.</note>, then you will find the perfect **Work** in the same, and rejoice. For **Albertus Magnus** <note>A famous 13th-century scholar and bishop rumored to have discovered the Philosopher's Stone.</note> says: this thing, from which the **Stone** is drawn, is possessed by both the poor and the rich: and it is **women’s work** and **child’s play** <note>A common alchemical phrase suggesting that once the matter is found, the process requires only patience and gentle heat, much like household chores.</note>, and its flower is the **Stone**.

Therefore, take this thing, even if it is already imperfect, for from the perfect nothing can become [new], for the **Species** <note>original: "Species," meaning the essential form or type of a substance.</note> or kinds of things are not changed by their nature, but rather corrupted: and yet it should not be entirely imperfect, for from something purely imperfect, nothing can come either. For **Art** cannot introduce or provide the first **dispositions** <term>Dispositiones: the inherent qualities or tendencies of a substance that allow it to be transformed.</term>. Rather, it is a **middle-thing** between the perfect and imperfect bodies. Since **Nature** does not make the imperfect ones perfect, but—

## Following is how to proceed in the second degree of Redness.

The second degree of **Redness** <note>original: "Röthe"; the Rubedo, the final stage of the alchemical process where the Stone reaches its full power.</note>, however (which is the fifth in the overall order), must be governed in all things—in the heat of the **dung** <note>original: "Mistes"; referring to a *balneum mariae* or a horse-dung bath, which provided a steady, gentle heat through fermentation.</note> and of the fire—during the **dissolution** <note>original: "solution"</note>, **coagulation**, **roasting** <note>original: "assation"</note>, and **fixation** <note>Making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates when heated.</note>, just as was maintained in the second degree of the **Whiteness** <note>original: "Weisse"; the Albedo or silver stage.</note>. And if, in this fifth degree of Redness, the thickness of the **oil** <note>A purified, liquid alchemical essence.</note> appears to you, proceed with it in every way as you did above in the first degree of Redness.

## Following is the manner in which to proceed in the third degree.

The third degree of Redness (which is the sixth in the order) should be governed with a stronger heat of the fire during the dissolution, roasting, coagulation, and fixation, similar to the fire that was maintained in the third degree of Whiteness. For the dung should be boiling, yet with less volatility, so that the **lights** <note>original: "Lichter"; likely referring to the volatile spirits or the luminous qualities of the substance as it nears perfection.</note> are joined together, and that the **sublimation**, **inceration** <note>original: "Inceration"; the process of softening a substance until it has a wax-like consistency.</note>, and fixation occur with a stronger fire than in the other two degrees of Redness. And if in this third degree the thickness of the oil appears to you, do in all things as you have done in the first and second degrees of Redness.

# Following is the Process for the Fourth Degree of Redness.

The fourth degree of **Redness** <note>original: "Röthe"; the Rubedo, the final stage of the Great Work.</note> (which is called the seventh in the sequence of degrees) is governed entirely like the third degree of Redness (which is called the sixth in the sequence of degrees); they are only different in this regard: in this fourth degree of Redness, the **oil** <note>original: "Oel"; the purified liquid essence or tincture.</note> is not divided after the **dissolution** <note>original: "solution"; the process of liquefying a solid substance.</note>, but is instead completely **coagulated** <note>original: "coaguliret"; the process of thickening or solidifying a liquid substance through heat.</note> with the **substance** <note>original: "Substanz"; the physical "body" of the alchemical matter.</note>. Otherwise, the procedure is followed in all respects as was described for the third degree of Redness. And let these few words be enough for making our **Philosophical Stone** <note>original: "Philosophischen Stein"; the ultimate goal of alchemy, believed to transmute base metals into gold and act as a universal medicine.</note>, to the praise and honor of Almighty **God**.

## Now follows the Governance of the Fire.

In the governance of the fire consists the entire art and science of the philosophers. Therefore, it is to be known that the first degree of the **Whiteness** <note>The *albedo* stage, where the matter is purified to a brilliant white.</note> is governed by a warmth that is, as it were, bubbling or simmering. The second degree of the Whiteness is governed like a manure-bed <note>original: "Mist"; alchemists often used the steady, gentle heat produced by fermenting horse manure as a natural incubator for their flasks.</note>, and this should not be too moist, yet it should possess a simmering warmth.

The third degree of the Whiteness, however, is governed such that the manure-bed is seething or boiling, yet with less moisture. And if the governance of the manure-bed seems too difficult for you to manage, then you should have pots into which you place the manure, according to the specific nature of the order or degree—whether warm, or as if simmering, or a fully boiling-hot heat. In these pots, alongside the manure, place your well-sealed glass vessel. When you begin to work in each respective degree, the pots should stand buried in deep manure up to their necks. The warmer they stand, the better governance of the fire you will have in the pots, so that you may ascend according to the teaching of the degrees and their proper order. This is done so that the charcoal fire is as gentle as the flame of a lamp, allowing you to ascend step-by-step <note>original: "Stuffen-Weiße (per gradus)"; the Latin *per gradus* emphasizes the incremental nature of the heating process.</note> through all degrees, just as the text of the three white degrees teaches.

### Here follows the shortening of the work without the addition of the raw powder.

Whoever wishes to make our work shorter without the addition of the raw powder or the raw *Bernas* <note>original: "Bernas"; likely a variation of "Borax" or a specific alchemical salt used as a flux or intermediary agent.</note>, let him do as follows:

When you have achieved the first degree of the **Whiteness** through the *solution* <note>original: "Solution"; the process of dissolving a solid substance into a liquid state.</note>, such that one pound is dissolved, then divide that pound into two parts. *Coagulate* <note>original: "coagulire"; to thicken or solidify a liquid into a solid mass.</note> one part according to the Whiteness of the first degree of the Whiteness, and set the other half aside, and also keep the dissolved oil. Then pour [the oil] onto the roasted matter <note>The "roasted" or calcined material resulting from the previous heating stages.</note> once without specific weight, and moisten it so that it barely becomes damp, like a thick dough. After that, set it to dissolve; subsequently, dry the dissolved matter in the sun or in a [warm] room. Afterward, *imbibe* <note>original: "imbibire"; the process of saturating a dry solid with a liquid until it can absorb no more.</note> it again, and then set it to *fix* <note>original: "figiren"; the alchemical process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat.</note> it, as the first order of the Whiteness teaches. You shall repeat this, and the volatile part shall be fixed by the stable part, and it shall flow [melt] upon a glowing metal plate. One part of this substance *tinges* <note>original: "tingiret"; from the Latin *tingere*, meaning to dye or transform the nature of a metal.</note> ten parts of the [base] bodies, but in *Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurio"; quicksilver.</note> it tinges forty parts into the finest silver. When the first degree of the Whiteness is thus accomplished, one proceeds with that very same substance to the second degree of the Whiteness, namely by moistening it with the reserved oil, without weighing, so that it barely becomes damp,

# The Glory of the World.

...dissolved and the <term>oil</term> <note>In alchemy, an "oil" is a liquid essence or "soul" of a substance, not a culinary oil.</note> has been transformed with the <term>oil</term> in the third <term>degree of Whiteness</term> <note>Alchemical stages are often measured in degrees or colors; "Whiteness" (albedo) indicates the stage where the matter can transmute base metals into silver.</note>, then divide the <term>oil</term> again into two parts, as was described in the second <term>degree of Whiteness</term>. **Coagulate** <term>coagulire: to thicken or solidify a liquid into a solid mass</term> one part with the fire of a lamp, as is said in the third <term>degree of Whiteness</term>, and then roast it. **Imbibe** <term>imbibire: the process of saturating a dry solid with a liquid until it can absorb no more</term> the roasted matter and **fix** <term>figire: the alchemical process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat</term> it in the third degree of Whiteness, until it is entirely **fixed** and flows without smoke upon a glowing [hot] metal plate.

And then one part of it **tinctures** <note>original: "tingiret"; the act of the alchemical "philosopher's stone" transforming a larger mass of base metal into a noble one through contact.</note> one hundred parts of any body [metal], and two hundred parts of **mercury** into the finest silver. 

When the third order is also completed, you shall proceed to the fourth <term>degree of Redness</term> <note>The "Redness" (rubedo) is the final and most powerful stage of the alchemical process, capable of producing gold.</note>. **Imbibe** this part again—a portion with the <term>oil</term> kept back from the third <term>degree of Whiteness</term>—and set it to **dissolve** <term>solviren: to break down a solid into liquid form</term> in the **manure** <note>original: "Mist"; alchemists often used the steady, gentle heat produced by rotting horse manure (called "venter equinus" or horse’s belly) as a natural incubator.</note>, until it is completely **dissolved** (as the second <term>degree of Whiteness</term> teaches) and transformed into <term>oil</term>.

Then divide this <term>oil</term> again into two parts: **coagulate** one part with the fire of the lamp, as the second <term>degree of Whiteness</term> teaches, and keep the other part. Thus **distill** and **coagulate** until it is **fixed** and flows upon a glowing plate without smoke. Then one part of it **tinctures** three thousand parts of any body [metal], and five thousand parts of raw **mercury** into the finest gold, which stands and endures in all trials. 

But you should know that if you wished to **dissolve** it further, you could not do it otherwise...

**Albini (Bernh. Siegfr.)** On the Bones of the Human Body, for his Students <note>original: "de Ossibus corporis humani, ad Auditores suos"</note>, 8. 1746. <term>8.: short for "octavo," a book size where each sheet of paper is folded into eight leaves, resulting in a medium-sized handbook.</term> <note>Bernhard Siegfried Albinus was a famous 18th-century German anatomist known for his highly accurate and artistic anatomical plates.</note>

**Book of Androphilus Asclepiadeus**, in which a few things are explained, by the knowledge of which health can be preserved and the life of man can be safe from the ignorance of doctors <note>original: "Androphili Asclepiadei Liber, in quo pauca explicantur, quorum scitu Sanitas conservari & vita hominis ab ignorantia Medicorum poterit esse secura"</note>, 8. 1748. <note>"Androphilus Asclepiadeus" is a pseudonym; the title reflects a common 18th-century skepticism toward the official medical establishment.</note>

**Contagious Plague**, which crept into Austria in the year 1713, along with the remedies serving against it, 8. <note>This refers to the Great Plague of Vienna, one of the last major outbreaks of the Black Death in the region.</note>

**Dietary Articles of Bratislava of the Year 1715** <note>original: "Articuli diætales Posonienses Anni 1715"</note>, fol. <term>fol.: short for "folio," a large book format where the paper is folded only once.</term> <note>These "dietary articles" were likely legal and health regulations passed by the Hungarian Diet (parliament) meeting in Bratislava (Pozsony) to manage public health after the plague.</note>

**Mr. George Berkeley’s** Report on Tar-Water, its preparation and use as well as wondrous effects in almost all diseases, 8. 1748. <note>George Berkeley was a famous Irish philosopher who became obsessed with the medicinal properties of water infused with pine tar, promoting it as a "panacea" or universal cure.</note>

**Bensæ (Franc. Xav.)** Historical Account of the Plague of the 12th, 13th, and 14th Years of this Century Infecting Austria and Neighboring Parts <note>original: "Historica Relatio Pestis Anni hujus Sæculi XII. XIII. & XIV. Austriam & conterminas partes infestantis"</note>, 8. Vienna 1717. <note>Franciscus Xaverius Bensa was a court physician in Vienna who documented the epidemic in detail.</note>
